query: Consider the following context: Constituent phases and their corresponding phase transformations are important in developing alloys. In that context, which method can be used for control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A machine learning framework trained on historical composition–process–structure–property data can predict optimal heat-treatment profiles that more reliably control the phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys compared to traditional trial-and-error approaches.
generation.material_initial_state: An Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy exhibiting a baseline microstructure with mixed or transitional phases following conventional processing.
generation.intervention: Apply heat-treatment profiles as predicted by the ML model, which specify targeted temperatures, pressures, and cooling rates to stabilize desired phases.
generation.conditions: Controlled thermal treatment environments (e.g., furnace conditions with precisely maintained temperatures, controlled atmospheres, and programmed cooling) where process variables are reproducibly maintained.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and refined morphology of constituent phases (such as B2, A2, FCC, or other ordered domains) that mediate the alloy’s mechanical and functional properties.
generation.mechanism: The machine learning model leverages large datasets from previous experiments to capture complex interactions between composition, processing conditions, and resulting microstructures. By predicting sensitive heat-treatment parameters, the intervention aims to guide nucleation and growth kinetics toward a more desirable phase distribution.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples processed using the ML-predicted heat-treatment profiles will exhibit a higher fraction of the desired phase(s) with controlled morphology, leading to improved or targeted mechanical/functional properties relative to those treated using conventional methods.
generation.baseline: Heat treatments determined by manual, iterative trial-and-error methods lacking systematic predictive power.
generation.boundary: The success of the approach may be limited by the quality and breadth of the historical data available and may require further refinement when applied to compositions or processing regimes outside the trained dataset.
generation.uncertainty: While early studies and data mining strategies suggest potential improvements, the absolute degree of phase control and property enhancement achievable through this method under varied practical processing conditions remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA samples and divide them into two groups. One group will be subjected to heat treatments based on ML-model predictions, while the control group will undergo traditional trial-and-error heat treatments. The samples will then be analyzed for phase composition and microstructure using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and transmission electron microscopy, and mechanical properties (e.g., strength and ductility) will be measured.
measurements: Quantitative phase fraction analysis via XRD
Mechanical property tests such as tensile strength and ductility measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-guided heat-treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in targeted phase fractions and corresponding mechanical/functional properties compared to the control group, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Discovering novel high entropy alloys (HEAs) with exceptional performance has ushered in a new era for materials design [1] – [3] . The melting temperature is a crucial parameter in the search for such materials. For instance, a correlation between a high melting point and elevated temperature strength has been identified in refractory complex concentrated alloys [4] . Besides the melting temperature, other melting properties, such as enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point, are also crucial for constructing phase diagrams and developing novel materials. However, experimental measurements on these properties, even for unary refractory materials, face severe challenges due to high melting points, often resulting in very scattered experimental data, if available at all. Additionally, the vast compositional space of HEAs makes systematic experimental screening of promising candidates impractical.

The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

decision.trend: Early work (2016) on AlxCoCrFeNi showed that increasing Al content shifted the alloy from single-phase to multiphase, with distinct precipitation behavior under irradiation in B2, A2, and fcc regions. Later (2024), systematically applying high-pressure, high-temperature treatment demonstrated that refining hierarchical phases in Al0.7CoCrFeNi could achieve both high strength and ductility. Most recently (2025), stepwise aging studies on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 revealed that thermal treatments can induce or mitigate embrittlement by tuning, for example, L12 domain size and phase boundary characteristics. Across these efforts, controlling the precise fraction and morphology of each phase remains difficult, particularly as composition and processing routes become more complex.
decision.unsolved: A fully predictive, reliable way to choose thermal or thermo-mechanical parameters for achieving target phase equilibria and morphologies in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni remains elusive. Although specific treatment schedules yield improved properties, a single generalized method for systematically determining ideal parameters across the broad composition space is still lacking.
decision.lever: Train a machine learning framework on existing composition–process–structure–property data to quickly predict optimal heat-treatment profiles that stabilize desired phases in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni.
decision.why: Data-driven modeling can handle the high complexity of multi-phase HEAs by learning from past experimental outcomes and guiding new experiments, thus offering a path toward more predictive and systematic phase control in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys.
